cards.title: Marriage and checkerboard · mapping a shared pairing constraint
cards.aim: Can a solver see why 31 pairs are impossible when the two groups are unequal?
cards.manipulated: The number of men and women (32 and 32, then 30 and 32), and the matching board problem with two same-colored corners removed.
cards.measured: Whether 31 heterosexual marriages (or 31 dominoes) can be formed.
cards.found: No. With 30 men and 32 women, at most 30 marriages are possible. The checkerboard has the same imbalance between square colors, so 31 dominoes cannot cover it.
cards.means: The solution comes from the one-of-each pairing relationship, not from total size or area.
cards.trap: Total count (62 people or 62 squares) says 31 pairs, but the pairing rule is what decides it.

cards.title: Duncker and Gick–Holyoak · radiation, fortress, and reminders
cards.aim: Do people notice and use a solved source story (the fortress) to solve the radiation problem?
cards.manipulated: Whether participants read the fortress story first, and whether they were told to think about that story.
cards.measured: Whether participants reached the converging-rays solution to the radiation problem.
cards.found: About 10% solved radiation without the analogy. After reading the fortress story, about 30% solved it. When told to think about the story, about 75% did.
cards.means: Having a useful source in memory is not enough. People must notice it and map it to the target.
cards.trap: Many people read the source but do not spontaneously use it. The hint is the difference between 30% and 75%.

cards.title: Lightbulb transfer · surface and structural similarities
cards.aim: Does a source with similar surface features, or similar structure, help solve a target problem?
cards.manipulated: Which source participants knew: radiation, fragile-glass lightbulb, or insufficient-intensity lightbulb. A control group had no source.
cards.measured: Whether participants solved the target (lightbulb or radiation).
cards.found: 81% who knew radiation solved the lightbulb problem, versus 10% in the control group. 69% who read the fragile-glass solution solved radiation, versus 33% after the insufficient-intensity version.
cards.means: Matching structure (a strong effect at the target plus protected surroundings) helps more than matching only the objects.
cards.trap: Both lightbulb sources use converging lasers, but only the fragile-glass one shares the reason (damage to surroundings).

cards.title: In vivo observation · analogies in scientific work
cards.aim: How often do real scientists use analogies during ordinary work?
cards.manipulated: Nothing was manipulated. Researchers observed scientists in real-world lab meetings.
cards.measured: The number of analogies used in a one-hour laboratory meeting.
cards.found: Scientists use about 3-15 analogies in a one-hour laboratory meeting.
cards.means: Analogies are common in real work even though they are hard to transfer in lab tasks (the analogical paradox).
cards.trap: In vivo gives real context but little control of variables, and it can be time-consuming.

cards.title: Chase and Simon · game positions, random layouts, and chunks
cards.aim: Is expert chess recall due to general memory or to organized knowledge?
cards.manipulated: Skill (chess master versus a beginner with under 100 hours) and the arrangement type (actual game positions versus random arrangements).
cards.measured: Reproducing the piece positions after viewing the board for five seconds.
cards.found: The expert did much better than the beginner on actual game positions. The same familiar chunks were not available for random arrangements.
cards.means: Expert memory depends on chunks stored in long-term memory, not on a general memory advantage.
cards.trap: Do not say experts remember everything better. The advantage is tied to meaningful positions.

cards.title: Chi and colleagues · surface-based and principle-based sorting
cards.aim: Do experts and novices organize physics problems in the same way?
cards.manipulated: Group: experts (physics professors) versus novices (students with one semester of physics).
cards.measured: Sorting 24 physics problems into groups by similarity.
cards.found: Novices grouped by surface features, such as inclined planes. Experts grouped by structural features, such as conservation of energy.
cards.means: Expertise changes which relationship is used as the basis for similarity.
cards.trap: The same problem 24 pairs with 23 (novice, inclined planes) or with 21 (expert, conservation of energy).

cards.title: Availability judgments · letter positions and causes of death
cards.aim: Do people judge how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind?
cards.manipulated: The letter question (r first versus r third) and paired causes of death (for example, botulism versus asthma).
cards.measured: Choosing which alternative is more frequent or more likely.
cards.found: About 70% say more words begin with r, though words with r third are three times more common. Many pick the dramatic cause of death over the more common one such as asthma.
cards.means: Ease of remembering is used as a cue for probability, and it is affected by things other than frequency.
cards.trap: Memorable or newsworthy is not the same as common.

cards.title: Representativeness · Robert, Jack, and Linda
cards.aim: Do people use resemblance instead of base rates and probability rules?
cards.manipulated: The description given (Robert, Jack, Linda) and whether base-rate information was available.
cards.measured: Judging occupation (librarian or farmer; engineer or lawyer) or choosing between bank teller and feminist bank teller.
cards.found: Many call Robert a librarian despite about 2.2 million farms versus 120,000 libraries. People use the 70/30 base rate alone but ignore it once Jack is described. About 82% choose the conjunction for Linda.
cards.means: A fitting description can override base rates and the conjunction rule.
cards.trap: Feminist bank teller is a subset of bank teller, so it cannot be more probable.

cards.title: Hospital samples · extreme proportions and sample size
cards.aim: Do people consider sample size when judging how often extreme proportions occur?
cards.manipulated: Hospital size: about 45 births per day versus about 15 births per day.
cards.measured: Choosing which hospital has more days with over 60% boys (larger, smaller, or about the same).
cards.found: 56% chose about the same. The correct answer is the smaller hospital, because small samples vary more.
cards.means: Small samples are more variable, which is why the law of large numbers matters.
cards.trap: The question is about days over 60%, not total boys born.

cards.title: Lord and colleagues · myside bias in article evaluation
cards.aim: Does an existing opinion change how the same evidence is evaluated?
cards.manipulated: Participants' opinion on capital punishment: in favor versus opposed.
cards.measured: How each participant interpreted the same article.
cards.found: Each side saw the article as favorable to its own position.
cards.means: Myside bias is evaluating evidence in a way that favors one's own opinions and attitudes.
cards.trap: Both groups read the same article. The difference is in the readers.

cards.title: Hidden number rule · confirmation and diagnostic tests
cards.aim: Do people look for evidence that could prove their hypothesis wrong?
cards.manipulated: Nothing varied between groups. Participants wrote their own number triples starting from 2, 4, 6.
cards.measured: Their triples and the rule they proposed, with feedback on whether each fit the experimenter's rule.
cards.found: The most common hypothesis was increasing intervals of two. The actual rule was three numbers in increasing order.
cards.means: Testing only triples that fit the hypothesis keeps a too-narrow belief alive. Testing for contradictions is more useful.
cards.trap: Repeated 'yes' feedback does not separate the narrow rule from the broader one.

cards.title: Jellybeans · favorable counts versus winning probability
cards.aim: Do people choose by the number of winning items or by the probability of winning?
cards.manipulated: Two bowls: 1 red bean out of 10 versus 7 red beans out of 100.
cards.measured: Which bowl participants chose before drawing.
cards.found: Most chose the 7-out-of-100 bowl, though 10% beats 7%.
cards.means: A larger count of favorable items draws attention away from the total number of draws.

cards.title: Ritov and Baron · convoy rerouting and lives saved
cards.aim: Do people choose the option that saves the most lives when it requires causing harm?
cards.manipulated: Rerouting a food convoy (saves 1,000 at the second camp, 100 die at the first) versus keeping the route.
cards.found: 63% did not choose to reroute. Some would keep the route even if only one person would die after the change.
cards.means: Reluctance to cause harm can outweigh a larger benefit, so choices are not just about the biggest number.
cards.trap: Net lives saved (900) favors rerouting, yet most refused.

cards.title: Tetlock and colleagues · taboo and tragic outcomes
cards.researcher: Tetlock, Kristel, Elson, Green, and Lerner (2000)
cards.aim: How do taboo and tragic tradeoffs affect moral outrage?
cards.manipulated: Tradeoff type (taboo: Johnny's life versus hospital money; tragic: two children, one liver) and outcome (Johnny saved or not saved).
cards.found: In the taboo tradeoff, not saving Johnny produced much greater outrage than saving him. In the tragic tradeoff, outrage was similar whether he was saved or not.
cards.means: The effect of the decision depends on the type of value conflict (an interaction).
cards.trap: A tragic tradeoff compares two sacred values. A taboo tradeoff puts a sacred value against a secular benefit.

cards.title: Ginges and colleagues · payment, recognition, and sacred commitments
cards.aim: How do people react to compromise deals over contested issues, and does money help?
cards.manipulated: Deal type: taboo, Taboo+ (one billion dollars a year for ten years), and symbolic (recognition and an apology). Participants were also classified as moral absolutists or not.
cards.measured: Anger, disgust, and support for violence.
cards.found: For moral absolutists, adding money increased anger, disgust, and support for violence. Non-absolutists responded the other way. Symbolic recognition lowered anger or disgust and violence support.
cards.means: Money can backfire when the issue is sacred, and symbolic reciprocity can help.
cards.trap: Samples were 601 settlers, 535 refugees, and 719 students.

cards.title: Iranian online study · sacred values, funds, sanctions, and energy results
cards.researcher: Dehghani, Atran, and colleagues (2010); Dehghani, Iliev, and colleagues (2009)
cards.aim: Do incentives or sanctions make Iranians who hold a sacred value more willing to give up the nuclear program?
cards.manipulated: A 2 x 3 design: program type (energy or weapons) by deal type (Taboo, Taboo+ with 40 billion dollars, Taboo- with the threat of sanctions).
cards.measured: Personal approval, anticipated public anger if the government approved, and whether the deal seems misleading.
cards.found: For sacred-value participants in the energy condition, approval was lower with funds or sanctions than with the basic deal, and anger was highest with funds. Participants without a sacred value rated approval higher and anger lower.
cards.means: For a sacred commitment, improving the material balance does not make a deal more acceptable.
cards.trap: Sacred means refusing the exchange no matter how great the consequences. About 14% (energy) and 13% (weapons) did so.

contrasts.title: Availability heuristic vs representativeness heuristic

a.definition: Judging how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind.

b.definition: Judging whether A belongs to class B by how much A resembles B.

contrasts.tell: Ask what supplies the shortcut. Remembered examples means availability. Similarity to a type means representativeness.
contrasts.example: Botulism in the news (availability) versus Robert resembling a librarian (representativeness).

contrasts.title: Surface features vs structural features

a.definition: The specific elements of a problem, such as a fortress, a tumor, or a ray.

b.definition: The underlying principle that governs the solution.

contrasts.tell: Surface is what the objects are. Structure is why a solution works.
contrasts.example: Lightbulb and laser are surface. A strong beam harming the surroundings is structural.

contrasts.title: Noticing vs mapping vs applying an analogy

a.definition: Recognizing that a source problem may be relevant to the target.

b.definition: Linking elements of the source to the target, then using that link to build a solution.

contrasts.tell: Noticing is finding the source. Mapping is lining up the parts. Applying is using them.
contrasts.example: About 30% solved radiation after the fortress story, and about 75% when told to think about it.

contrasts.title: Analogical source vs target

a.definition: A problem with relevant similarities whose solution guides a new problem.

contrasts.tell: The target is what you need to solve now. The source is what you already know.
contrasts.example: Russian marriage is the source and the mutilated checkerboard is the target.

contrasts.title: Base rate vs description information

a.definition: The background prevalence of categories, such as 70 lawyers and 30 engineers.

b.definition: Personal characteristics, such as Jack's hobbies, that resemble a category.

contrasts.tell: Base rate says how common the category is. The description says how well the person fits it.
contrasts.example: People use 70/30 alone but call Jack an engineer once he is described.

contrasts.title: Conjunction rule vs representativeness

a.definition: The probability of two events together cannot exceed either one alone.

b.definition: Seeing a more detailed, better-fitting story as more probable.

contrasts.tell: The rule is about nested sets. Representativeness is about fit.
contrasts.example: About 82% chose feminist bank teller over bank teller for Linda.

contrasts.title: Confirmation bias vs myside bias

a.definition: Seeking information that fits a hypothesis and overlooking what argues against it.

b.definition: Generating and evaluating evidence, and testing hypotheses, in ways biased toward one's own opinions and attitudes.

contrasts.tell: Myside bias is one form of confirmation bias, tied to one's own opinions and attitudes.

contrasts.title: Taboo tradeoff vs tragic tradeoff

a.definition: Mixes sacred and secular domains, such as a child's life against money.

b.definition: Compares two sacred values with each other.

contrasts.tell: Ask whether the competing item is a secular benefit (taboo) or another sacred value (tragic).
contrasts.example: Johnny's liver costing one million dollars versus two children and one liver.

contrasts.title: Moral absolutists vs non-absolutists

a.definition: Treat the issue as a sacred value and reject compromise regardless of benefit.

b.definition: Have strong preferences against compromise but do not treat the issue as sacred.

contrasts.tell: Ask whether benefits can enter the decision at all, not how much the person cares.
contrasts.example: Adding money to Taboo+ raised anger for absolutists and lowered it for non-absolutists.

contrasts.title: Material incentive vs symbolic recognition

a.definition: Money added to the deal, such as one billion dollars a year for ten years.

b.definition: Recognition of the other group's right and an apology, with no added cash.

contrasts.tell: Money changes the economic benefit. Symbolic terms address the status of a group's claim.
contrasts.example: Taboo+ raised absolutists' anger, while the symbolic offer lowered anger and support for violence.

contrasts.title: Incentive (Taboo+) vs disincentive (Taboo-)

a.definition: A benefit offered for agreeing, such as 40 billion dollars in funds.

b.definition: A cost imposed for refusing, such as additional sanctions.

contrasts.tell: Incentives change the benefit of accepting. Disincentives change the cost of refusing.
contrasts.example: Iran study: Taboo+ gave funds and Taboo- threatened sanctions.

contrasts.title: Expert vs novice problem organization

a.definition: Group problems by structural features, such as conservation of energy.

b.definition: Group problems by surface features, such as inclined planes.

contrasts.tell: Novices go by what the problem looks like. Experts go by the principle that solves it.
contrasts.example: Chi et al. (1982): problems 23 and 24 (novice) versus 21 and 24 (expert).

questions: What is the difference between a source problem and a target problem?
In the Russian marriage problem, what do the marriages and the groups of people correspond to in the checkerboard problem?
What solution did Duncker's radiation problem require, and what percentage solved it without the analogy?
Which concept is this an example of: sending small groups along different roads so they arrive together at the fortress?
How did the percentage solving radiation change after reading the fortress story, and after being told to think about it?
ask.remember: Both the fortress and radiation solutions use weak approaches that converge to give a strong effect at one target. Noticing the source is the hard step.

ask.topic: Noticing, surface similarity, and structural correspondence
questions: What did 81% versus 10% show in the lightbulb study?
What is the difference between surface features and structural features?
Why did the fragile-glass source (69%) help more than the insufficient-intensity source (33%) on radiation?
What is analogical encoding?
Which concept is this: noticing, mapping, or applying: connecting the central target to the separate approaches?
ask.remember: Matching structure (a strong effect at the target and protected surroundings) matters more than matching objects, though similar surfaces help noticing.

questions: What is the analogical paradox?
How many analogies do scientists use in a one-hour lab meeting?
What is in vivo problem-solving research?
What is one tradeoff of in vivo research compared with a lab experiment?
ask.remember: Analogies are hard to transfer in the lab but common in real work (about 3-15 per meeting). In vivo trades control for real context.

ask.topic: Expert knowledge, chunks, and problem organization
questions: What did Chase and Simon (1973) find about experts and random chess arrangements?
What is a chunk?
How did novices and experts sort the physics problems in Chi et al. (1982)?
Which concept explains why an expert groups problems 21 and 24 together?
Do experts outperform novices outside their field?
ask.remember: Experts rely on organized knowledge (chunks, principles) within their field. Outside the field they are no better than novices.

ask.topic: Creativity, divergent thinking, and implementing solutions
questions: What is divergent thinking?
What stages come after generating ideas in creative problem solving?
How can too much knowledge hinder creative problem solving?
What does thinking flexibly require when a familiar procedure does not fit?
ask.remember: Ideas are necessary but not enough. Evaluation, planning, and implementation are separate parts. Familiar procedures can block flexibility.

questions: What is the difference between decisions and reasoning?
What is inductive reasoning?
What three things determine the strength of an inductive argument?
How does the black swan example show the weight of one high-quality observation?
Why are inductive conclusions only probably true?
ask.remember: Decisions choose between alternatives. Reasoning draws conclusions. Induction goes from observations to probable conclusions.

questions: What did people choose in the r-first versus r-third word question, and what is the truth?
What is base-rate neglect, and how does the Jack problem show it?
Why is choosing feminist bank teller for Linda a conjunction error?
What is the correct answer to the hospital question, and why?
What does the law of large numbers say?
ask.remember: Availability uses ease of remembering. Representativeness uses resemblance. Small samples vary more than large ones.

ask.topic: Illusory correlation, myside bias, and hypothesis testing
questions: What is an illusory correlation?
How does a stereotype connect to the availability heuristic?
What did Lord and colleagues (1979) find about people who favored or opposed capital punishment?
What is the difference between confirmation bias and myside bias?
What was the actual rule in the 2, 4, 6 task, and what hypothesis was most common?
ask.remember: People look for and favor information that fits what they already believe, and rarely test what could disprove it.

ask.topic: Utility, probabilities, and choices that cause harm
questions: What does expected utility theory assume people do?
Why do utility procedures not fully describe real choices (for example, casino gambling)?
In the jellybean choice, which bowl did most people pick and which has the higher probability?
What did Ritov and Baron (1999) find about rerouting the convoy?
How did avoiding air travel after September 11 increase harm?
ask.remember: People do not always maximize expected benefit. They are swayed by counts, harm avoidance, and fear.

ask.topic: Sacred values, taboo and tragic tradeoffs
questions: What is a sacred value, and how is it kept separate from secular values?
What is the difference between a taboo tradeoff and a tragic tradeoff?
What did Tetlock and colleagues (2000) find about outrage when Johnny was not saved in each tradeoff?
Which tradeoff produced similar outrage whether Johnny was saved or not?
ask.remember: Taboo mixes sacred with secular and causes outrage. Tragic compares two sacred values, so outcome matters less.

questions: Who were the participants in Ginges, Atran, Medin, and Shikaki (2007)?
What was added in Taboo+, and what was added in the symbolic version?
How did moral absolutists and non-absolutists differ in response to money?
What percentage of settlers held the sacred-value position on the Land of Israel?
How did symbolic recognition compare with money for anger and support for violence?
ask.remember: For sacred issues money can backfire (more anger and support for violence), while symbolic reciprocity helps.

ask.topic: Nuclear-program study, manipulations, measures, and energy results
questions: What is the design of the Iranian online study (Dehghani and colleagues)?
What do Taboo, Taboo+, and Taboo- each involve?
How was a sacred value classified, and how many participants did so?
What did sacred-value participants show for approval and anger with funds or sanctions in the energy condition?
What three judgments did participants make?
ask.remember: Funds and sanctions did not raise approval for sacred-value participants and raised anticipated anger. Non-sacred participants barely changed.

explainers.title: Pairing problems: marriage and checkerboard
explainers.plain: Count the two kinds of pieces that must pair up. If the counts differ, a full pairing is impossible.
steps: Find what each pair must contain (one man and one woman, or one square of each color).
Count each kind.
Compare the counts, not the total.
If unequal, some are left over, however you rearrange.
explainers.example: 30 men and 32 women give at most 30 marriages. Removing two same-colored corners leaves unequal colors, so 31 dominoes cannot cover the board.
explainers.watchOut: Do not use total size (62 divided by 2 = 31).

explainers.title: Converging solution (radiation, fortress, lightbulb)
explainers.plain: Split a strong effect into weak parts that travel separately and meet at the target.
steps: Find the target that needs a strong effect.
Find the limit on the paths (healthy tissue, mines, fragile glass).
Use several weak approaches from different directions.
Make them arrive together.
explainers.example: Several low-intensity rays hit the tumor at once. Each path is safe, and the combined intensity destroys it.
explainers.watchOut: Dividing without combining at the same time does not work.

explainers.title: Base rates and Jack
explainers.plain: Start with how common each category is, then adjust for the description, instead of ignoring the numbers.
steps: Write the base rate (70 lawyers, 30 engineers).
With no description, the chance of an engineer is 30 out of 100.
With a description, remember the group still has more lawyers.
Do not decide on fit alone.
explainers.example: Jack is conservative, careful, and enjoys home carpentry and math puzzles. People say engineer, yet the group is 70 lawyers.
explainers.watchOut: A good-fitting description does not settle the probability.

explainers.title: Conjunction rule (Linda)
explainers.plain: Adding a condition can only shrink the set, so a combination is never more likely than one part.
steps: Name the two events (bank teller, feminist bank teller).
See that feminist bank tellers are inside bank tellers.
The smaller set cannot be more probable.
explainers.example: About 82% chose feminist bank teller, but bank teller alone must be at least as probable.
explainers.watchOut: A more detailed story feels more likely but is not.

explainers.title: Sample size (hospital question)
explainers.plain: Small samples swing more, so extreme proportions happen more often in them.
steps: Note the sample sizes (about 15 versus 45 births a day).
Note the true rate is about 50% boys in both.
Ask which sample can stray more from 50%.
Pick the smaller one.
explainers.example: The smaller hospital has more days over 60% boys. 56% wrongly said about the same.
explainers.watchOut: Do not confuse total boys with the share of days above 60%.

explainers.title: Probability as a ratio (jellybeans)
explainers.plain: Chance of winning is winning items divided by total items, not the count of winning items.
steps: Write each bowl as red out of total.
Convert to a percentage.
Compare the percentages.
explainers.example: 1 out of 10 is 10%. 7 out of 100 is 7%. So the first bowl is better, although most picked the second.
explainers.watchOut: A bigger count of red beans hides the larger total.

explainers.title: Expected utility
explainers.plain: Weigh how good each outcome is by how likely it is, then choose the best total.
steps: List the alternatives.
Rate the value of each outcome.
Combine value with chance.
Choose the maximum expected utility.
explainers.example: Casino gambling shows people choosing an activity despite knowing the odds are against them.
explainers.watchOut: People value things other than money, so the theory does not fully describe choices.

explainers.title: Inductive evidence strength
explainers.plain: Inductive conclusions are probably true, and they are stronger with better observations.
steps: Check how representative the observations are.
Check how many there are.
Check how good (compelling) each one is.
Allow that one strong case can contradict a claim.
explainers.example: Many white swans support the claim that all swans are white, but one clearly observed black swan contradicts it.
explainers.watchOut: More observations is not the only factor. Quality counts.
